results.title: An interesting experience
results.text:
This is such an experience and I can't really explain how I felt visiting it. Because in my own culture cremations and burials are very private affairs, I felt a little like a intruder into other people's grief. The ritual wailing of the women before the cremation was rather disturbing to me and it felt somewhat disrespectful to be wandering amidst so many families grieving for loved ones as they were being cremated right there in front of my own eyes.

Trusting that it was not disrespectful to the Hindu people (after all I'd been charged Rs1000 to go in and wasn't even asked not to take photos) I walked round the large site trying to take in as much of this interesting culture as I could. There were monkeys running around and cows roaming freely amongst the tourists and the mourning relatives of the deceased. The architecture and the history was fascinating.

Some of the young guides were a little insistent, but I did manage to persuade all 4 of the persistent young men who approached me, that for me this was more of a spiritual experience for which I appreciated having my own thoughts, and for whom only I could be my particular guide. Having said this, I'm sure these guides are very knowledgeable.

Certainly an interesting experience, though, due to the cremations, not one that everyone can stomach.

results.title: Worth a visit
results.text:
This is one of only a few Hindu temples we visited .. the rest mainly being Bhuddist. 
It is very interesting to see .. especially the bit near the river which is used for cremations and also checking out the row of towers which have been aligned in a row so you can look straight through. 
The only downside is that compared to other places of worship it is pretty dirty and given you have to remove your shoes to enter that does kind of put you off.

results.title: A must for every Hindu!
results.text:
Visited Nepal in Nov 2013. The main reason for the visit was the divine and holy Pashupatinath Temple. 
A very huge and beautiful main temple with smaller temples of different gods and goddesses around it. It is situated on the banks of the holy Bagmati river which is regarded as the Ganga of Nepal. Many rites and rituals are performed here on the banks of the river. 
The main deity Shri Pashupatinath is a big and totally divine Shivalinga with four heads.
The early morning and evening Arti is another major attraction. An extremely holy and spiritual experience, not to be missed.
A place i would love to visit again and again.Bam Bam Bhole!

results.text: This is a good place to see the law of nature and culture of the Indian people in Nepal. Instead of the going to Varanasi in India, this is a place to visit on a much smaller scale.

results.title: A Beautiful Temple of Lord Shiva
results.text: This temple complex is very big and Beautiful,and worth seeing .The temple like all other famous temples has a lot of security, due to the crowd they hardly let you see the deity even for a few  seconds,I wish I could have spent some more time inside the temple.We had done a pooja there which was quite nice but this is not done inside the temple but outside.and they give a mala of panchamukhi Rudraksha as prasad.

results.title: An atmosphere you wont find anywhere else!
results.text: We found this sunset visit simply amazing! So much going on- singing, drums, burning bodies- lots of pilgrims. The hospice just above the ghats was touching. We felt very privileged to see an alive temple with everyone doing their thing! The time of day added to the mystery but it got dark before we could see everything. We were able to see the back of the bull (not being Hindu) and walk around  most of the complex. We were befriended by a student who became our most competent guide and even walked us back to our hotel! Images and an atmosphere we will never forget....

results.title: A real experience but ....
results.text: Very pleased to visit the place again after eight years, it still has it's special atmosphere but what a pity the government decided to ask an entry fee of 1.000,- Nepalese roupies !!

results.title: Jawdropping!
results.text:
I was on a planned tour with a terrific local guide who talked me thru this large area, certain areas foreignors cannot enter but walking around the temples is enlighting, then he asked if I wanted to go to the crematorions, which it didn't dawn on me, until walking down the hill and seeing the bellowing smoke below.   Then I laid my eyes on 5 areas that were actually doing the cremations, and couldn't believe that this very private procedure back in the US is done out in the open, many onlookers from the opposite bank, able to take photos; no words to describe this, have to see for yourself.

After seeing this I was a little more prepared when I reached the River Ganges, in Varanasi India the next day and saw the same but closer.

Very interesting and compelling  to say the least.

results.title: same complex as the crematorium
results.text: It is a nice temple structure but there is just too much for the senses- visually you have live cremations to view, kids begging, hawkers selling trinkets, Holy men posing for pictures for donations- bottom line for me is that i don't think that a families grief and surrounding ceremonies are meant for tourists with cameras.

results.title: Dont miss the ghat behind the temple
results.text: A calm and serene place where you can the last journeys of the people. The old structures around, a small jungle at the back, the holy atmosphere adds to the aura of the place.

results.title: Confronting cremations of Pashupatinath
results.text:
I had heard about the cremations at Pashupatinath so had tried to prepare myself for it. The first thing to assualt the senses was the sight of an amusement park that is on the grounds. The large swinging pirate boat seemed strangely out of place. Perhaps this wouldn't be as real as I thought.You enter through a large gate that then becomes a largish path that winds its way up to the actual crematoria site. And yes it gets real. 
Passing by the sadhus etc, you come to the river where at any time of the day people can bring their relatives who have passed away to be cremated. There are platforms along the river where after ritual bathing/cleansing of the body the fires can be lit and the bodies can begin their reduction to ash. 
Its confronting to be so intimate in a strangers life as you see them grieving. But the process is highly ritualised and peaceful. 
The temple is filled with cows, and beggars and sadhus and grieving relatives, and a general sense of peace. 
You cannot enter the Hindu temple itself but are allowed to peer in, and can catch a glimpse of the extremely large testicles of a golden bull. 
Take the time to really see the whole site and appreciate all of the rituals that are happening. from the sons honouring their fathers deaths yearly, to the pilgrims coming to the biggest Hindu temple in Asia, to the locals digging pennies out of the ashes. 
For a site dedicated to death it is full of life and visually explosive.

results.title: A real eye-opener
results.text: Before visiting Pashupatinath I was concerned that it was using death and grief as entertainment for tourists.  I needn't have worried and I'm now very glad I have been there.  For a start, the whole approach to the temples is lined with a multitude of stalls seeling offerings. Hindus vastly outnumber tourists, and although the ghats are used for cremation, there is no intrusion upon the rituals and a good distance maintained between grieving families and ordinary visitors. The most sacred temple is reserved for Hindus only but the whole vast complex can be seen from the hill on the opposite side of the river so that you can begin to undertand how it all works. It is a quite extraordinary place.

results.title: Ash to ash....
results.text:
Firstly, the main sanctuary is prohibited to non Hindu. You can only stand at the main entrance. Photos at the entrance is permitted but not the inside. So, I may be at the most holiest place for Hindu but I can't get in.
If you can stomach to witness the funeral of the Hindu, then one may stay on. I will not elaborate on what I witnessed. Let's just stay its different and may be a wee bit primitive but it's their culture.
